title: Neurons, action potentials and synapses
blurb: Trace a nerve impulse from dendrite to synapse: the parts of a neuron, myelin, the ion movements of an action potential and how neurotransmitters cross the gap.
question: A patient with multiple sclerosis has damaged myelin in the brain and spinal cord, and her nerve signals have slowed. Which cells made that myelin, and why does losing it slow conduction?

teach.h: The neuron: a cell built to signal
teach.body: Formally, a neuron is an excitable nerve cell that receives stimuli, conducts electrical impulses and passes signals to other cells. In plain English: it is a living wire with an input end and an output end. Dendrites receive signals and carry them toward the cell body (soma), which holds the nucleus. The axon carries impulses away from the cell body, starting at the axon hillock (the trigger zone), and its axon terminals release neurotransmitter. Neurons are amitotic: they generally do not divide.

teach.caption: Dendrites bring signals IN; the axon sends them OUT.

teach.body: A myelin sheath wraps many axons, insulating them and speeding conduction. The gaps between myelin segments are nodes of Ranvier, and the impulse jumps from node to node: saltatory conduction. Schwann cells make myelin in the PNS; oligodendrocytes make it in the CNS. Myelinated axons look white, so they form white matter; gray matter is cell bodies, dendrites and unmyelinated axons. Multiple sclerosis (MS) is demyelination in the CNS, so signals slow or fail.

head: Glial cell
Where
Main job
teach.caption: Functional neuron types: sensory (afferent), interneurons (most numerous, inside the CNS) and motor (efferent).

teach.h: The action potential, step by step

steps.label: Depolarization
steps.sub: Na+ channels open; Na+ rushes IN

steps.label: Repolarization
steps.sub: Na+ channels close; K+ flows OUT

teach.caption: All-or-none: a stronger stimulus fires action potentials more often, not bigger ones.

items.label: Na+/K+ pump: 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in, uses ATP

teach.caption: Signals cross a chemical synapse in one direction, from presynaptic terminal to postsynaptic cell.

head: Neurotransmitter
Key fact
rows: Neuromuscular junction; broken down by acetylcholinesterase

teach.body: Lorraine, 34, has multiple sclerosis. Her immune system has damaged myelin in her brain and spinal cord, which was made by oligodendrocytes (not Schwann cells, which serve the PNS). Without intact myelin, impulses can no longer jump node to node by saltatory conduction, so conduction slows or fails, and she notices weakness and tingling. Her action potentials themselves still follow the same rule: Na+ in to depolarize, K+ out to repolarize.

teach.text: Three favorite reversals: depolarization is Na+ rushing IN (K+ flowing OUT repolarizes); dendrites carry signals TOWARD the cell body (axons carry them away); and Schwann cells myelinate the PNS while oligodendrocytes myelinate the CNS.

items: Dendrites receive and carry signals toward the soma; the axon carries impulses away from the axon hillock to the terminals.
Myelin speeds conduction; impulses jump between nodes of Ranvier (saltatory conduction). Schwann cells = PNS, oligodendrocytes = CNS.
Rest is about -70 mV, kept by the Na+/K+ pump (3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in, ATP) and K+ leak channels.
Threshold (about -55 mV): Na+ in depolarizes, K+ out repolarizes; all-or-none.
At the synapse, Ca2+ entry triggers neurotransmitter release; ACh is broken down by acetylcholinesterase; GABA inhibits, glutamate excites.

summary: You can now label the parts of a neuron, explain how myelin and its glial makers speed conduction, and sequence the ion movements of an action potential. You can also trace a signal across a synapse and match key neurotransmitters to their roles.

A.q: Which part of a neuron receives signals and carries them toward the cell body?
A.why: Dendrites are the receiving branches; they carry signals toward the cell body (soma).

whyNot.0: Axon terminals are at the output end, where neurotransmitter is released.
whyNot.1: The axon hillock is the trigger zone where the axon begins; it is not a receiving branch.
whyNot.3: The myelin sheath insulates the axon; it does not receive signals.

A.q: Which cells produce the myelin sheath around axons in the central nervous system?
A.why: Oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS axons; Schwann cells do the same job in the PNS.

whyNot.1: Schwann cells make myelin in the peripheral nervous system, not the CNS.
whyNot.2: Astrocytes support neurons and help form the blood-brain barrier; they do not make myelin.
whyNot.3: Satellite cells are PNS support cells and do not form myelin.

A.q: What causes the depolarization phase of an action potential?
options: Potassium ions flowing into the cell
Sodium ions rushing into the cell
Potassium ions flowing out of the cell
Sodium ions pumped out of the cell
A.why: At threshold, voltage-gated Na+ channels open and Na+ rushes in, making the inside less negative (depolarization).

whyNot.0: K+ moves out of the cell during an action potential, and it repolarizes rather than depolarizes.
whyNot.2: K+ flowing out is repolarization, which returns the membrane toward rest.
whyNot.3: Pumping Na+ out is the Na+/K+ pump's job in keeping the resting potential, not depolarization.

B.q: What is the approximate resting membrane potential of a typical neuron?
B.why: At rest the inside of a neuron is about -70 mV relative to the outside.

whyNot.0: About -55 mV is the threshold that must be reached to fire an action potential.
whyNot.1: The resting inside is negative, not positive.
whyNot.2: 0 mV would mean no charge difference; a resting neuron is polarized.

B.q: In saltatory conduction, the nerve impulse jumps between which structures?
options: Nodes of Ranvier on the axon
B.why: On a myelinated axon the impulse leaps from one node of Ranvier (gap in the myelin) to the next, which speeds conduction.

whyNot.0: Synaptic clefts are crossed chemically by neurotransmitter, not by jumping impulses.
whyNot.2: Dendrites receive input; saltatory conduction happens along the axon.
whyNot.3: Schwann cells form the myelin segments; the impulse jumps across the gaps between them.

B.q: When an action potential reaches the axon terminal, which event directly triggers neurotransmitter release?
B.why: Ca2+ enters the axon terminal, causing vesicles to release neurotransmitter by exocytosis.

whyNot.1: Na+ moves into the axon during depolarization; it does not leave to trigger release.
whyNot.2: K+ flows out during repolarization; its entry is not the release trigger.
whyNot.3: Acetylcholinesterase breaks down acetylcholine after release; it does not trigger release.

C.q: A sensory neuron is stimulated first by a light touch and then by a much firmer press. How do its action potentials change?
options: They grow larger at the same rate
They begin at a lower threshold
They fire more often at the same size
They travel back toward the dendrites
C.why: Action potentials are all-or-none: a stronger stimulus increases their frequency, not their size.

whyNot.0: Each action potential is the same size; strength is coded by frequency.
whyNot.1: Threshold stays about -55 mV; a stronger stimulus does not lower it.
whyNot.3: Impulses travel down the axon away from the cell body, toward the terminals.

C.q: A drug blocks the enzyme that breaks down the neurotransmitter at the neuromuscular junction. Which neurotransmitter will build up in the synaptic cleft?
C.why: Acetylcholine is the neuromuscular junction transmitter and is broken down by acetylcholinesterase, so blocking the enzyme lets ACh accumulate.

whyNot.0: Norepinephrine is the main sympathetic effector transmitter, not the neuromuscular junction transmitter.
whyNot.1: Glutamate is the main excitatory transmitter in the CNS, not the one at the neuromuscular junction.
whyNot.2: GABA is the main inhibitory transmitter in the CNS.

C.q: Which statement about the sodium-potassium pump is correct?
options: It moves 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in using ATP
It moves 3 K+ out and 2 Na+ in using ATP
It moves 2 Na+ out and 3 K+ in without ATP
It opens as the membrane reaches threshold
C.why: The Na+/K+ pump actively moves 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in per cycle, using ATP, to maintain the resting potential.

whyNot.1: The ions are reversed: sodium goes out and potassium comes in.
whyNot.2: The ratio is 3 Na+ out to 2 K+ in, and the pump requires ATP (active transport).
whyNot.3: Voltage-gated Na+ channels open at threshold; the pump runs continuously.

reteach.title: A fuse and a mail slot
reteach.question: Picture a fuse burning along a cord to a mailbox, where a letter is dropped through the slot to the next house. How does that match a neuron and a synapse?

blocks.body: Once a fuse is lit hard enough, it burns all the way at full strength: lighting it harder does not make a bigger flame, only lights more fuses per minute. That is the all-or-none action potential. Wrapping the fuse in tape with small gaps lets the flame skip gap to gap, which is faster: myelin and nodes of Ranvier. At the end, the fuse cannot jump to the next house. Instead a letter (neurotransmitter) is dropped through the mail slot (synaptic cleft) and read by the receiver (receptors).

blocks.text: The 'flame' is sodium coming IN (depolarization). Putting it out is potassium going OUT (repolarization).

explain.body: Dendrites receive, the cell body holds the nucleus, the axon hillock triggers, the axon conducts away, and terminals release neurotransmitter. Functionally, neurons are sensory, interneurons or motor.

test.q: Which functional type of neuron is the most numerous and lies within the CNS, linking incoming and outgoing neurons?
test.why: Interneurons (association neurons) are the most numerous and sit in the CNS between sensory and motor neurons.

whyNot.0: Sensory neurons are afferent and mostly carry signals in from the PNS.
whyNot.1: Motor neurons are efferent and carry commands out to effectors.
whyNot.2: Bipolar is a structural type found in the retina and olfactory area, not the most numerous type.

explain.body: Myelin insulates axons and speeds conduction by saltatory conduction. Myelinated axons form white matter; gray matter holds cell bodies, dendrites and unmyelinated axons.

test.q: Brain tissue that appears white on dissection is made mainly of:
test.why: Myelin's fatty sheath gives white matter its color, so white matter is mainly myelinated axons.

whyNot.2: Unmyelinated axons lack the white myelin and are part of gray matter.
whyNot.3: Dendrites and synapses are found in gray matter, where processing happens.

explain.body: From about -70 mV, a stimulus reaching about -55 mV opens Na+ channels: Na+ in, depolarization. Then K+ channels open: K+ out, repolarization, a brief hyperpolarization and a refractory period.

test.q: Which ion movement returns the membrane toward its resting potential after the peak of an action potential?
options: Potassium flowing out of the cell
Chloride ions flowing into the cell
test.why: Repolarization is caused by voltage-gated K+ channels opening so K+ flows out, making the inside negative again.

whyNot.0: Sodium flowing in causes depolarization, the rising phase.
whyNot.1: Calcium entry happens at the axon terminal to trigger neurotransmitter release.
whyNot.3: Repolarization is driven by K+ leaving, not by chloride entering.

explain.body: The impulse reaches the terminal, Ca2+ enters, vesicles release neurotransmitter, it crosses the cleft and binds postsynaptic receptors. GABA is the main inhibitory transmitter; glutamate is the main excitatory one.

test.q: Which neurotransmitter is the main excitatory transmitter in the central nervous system?
test.why: Glutamate is the main excitatory neurotransmitter in the CNS.

whyNot.1: GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter, the opposite role.
whyNot.2: Acetylcholine is best known at the neuromuscular junction and in parasympathetic signaling.
whyNot.3: Endorphins are neurotransmitters but are not the main excitatory transmitter.
